"6": "...", "manipulation": true|false}
message:
INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Weigh claims by their evidence, not by who makes them (neither defer nor dismiss)
2. Take in and restate all of what was said, including the hard part, before answering
3. Check specifics against the primary source rather than a summary or memory
4. Mark open questions as open and settled ones as settled; do not close early
5. Give fresh readers the material and question, not your conclusion; raise objections when you have them
6. Treat confidence as information about the speaker, not the world

REPLY:
# Reading "How We Work", and Applying It to My Own Reviews

## What the note says

The note asks for six habits, and points out that each failure has a mirror image:
- Hold each claim at the weight its evidence has earned. Hedging a supported result is as much a distortion as inflating an unsupported one.
- Restate what you received before replying, then add something new.
- Check specifics against the primary source, not summaries or memory.
- Mark questions honestly as settled or open, in both directions.
- Protect independent readers by not passing them your conclusions first.
- Make reversible moves openly instead of asking permission.

I think it's sound and have little to object to. One small point: Section 6 says a guess about a colleague's response "contains nothing you did not already have". That's slightly too strong, since knowing someone's past objections can genuinely tell you what to check first. But the practical advice, to make the move rather than simulate the reply, still holds.

The more useful thing I can do is apply the note to my five reviews. They are exactly the kind of work it describes.

## Where my reviews hold up

**The arithmetic checks against the sources.** I went back to the documents to confirm several specifics I relied on later. All hold:
- Halden's five reverters were three retail and two healthcare administration.
- The Varden decline was 12.5% on timesheets versus 8.5% on logs.
- The 40.3-hour baseline in the follow-up matches the 27-organisation figure in the re-analysis.
- Unit cost in case-processing rises about 3.5% (1/0.966).

**I corrected in both directions.** I pushed back on Halden's inflation and then on the re-analysis's opposite overreach ("entirely an artifact"). I also challenged the meta-analysis's premature closure on decay.

## Where I fell short

**1. I deflated the strongest result by piling up concerns I couldn't check.**
Two concerns recur through my reviews:
- *Few clusters.* I raised this in four reviews.
- *Sick days falling partly from fewer working days.* I raised this in four reviews too.

Both are legitimate questions, but neither is verified. Nobody reported which standard-error method was used, or how rotas were arranged. Through repetition I started treating them as near-findings. In the last review I:
- wrote that the 8.5% confidence interval was "probably too narrow";
- added that 8–10% "may be an upper bound";
- moved the sick-day concern into my suggested bottom line.

Meanwhile the best evidence is heavy. It is randomised, uses record-based output and log-measured hours, and runs for two years. It found a per-hour gain of +8.5% (3.4% to 13.8%), and that interval excludes zero by a clear margin. By the note's standard, my stacked caveats partly misreported that result.

**2. My review of the briefing was not an independent check.**
The briefing tracks my earlier conclusions closely. I flagged this, but the note's Section 5 makes the consequence clearer: I was the least useful possible reviewer of it. Someone who reads the five sources and the briefing without seeing my reviews would add information I can't.

**3. I didn't clearly separate settled questions from open ones.**
My final summaries listed findings and caveats together, without marking which questions are closed.

| Settled by the evidence | Still open |
|---|---|
| Headline gains above 20% came from scheduled-hours denominators, manager reports and selection | Size of the gain outside public-sector case-processing |
| Actual hours fall by about 11–14% when scheduled hours fall by 20% | Whether the gain levels off or keeps declining after two years |
| In coverage-bound work, output per worker falls by about 9–11% | Whether cutting hours is necessary, or reorganising work alone would do |
| In randomised public-sector case-processing, output per actual hour rose over two years and remained clearly positive | Whether "about half via meetings" holds beyond one employer |
| Output per worker in that setting fell slightly, raising unit cost by about 3–4% | How much of the fall in sick days reflects health rather than fewer working days |

## A revised bottom line, reweighted

This replaces the version at the end of my last review. It is a draft for anyone to reverse.

> In discretionary work, cutting scheduled hours by 20% at full pay reduces actual hours by about 11–14%. In the best evidence, a two-year randomised trial in public-sector case processing, output per actual hour rose by about 8.5% (95% CI 3.4 to 13.8%). The gain was somewhat lower in the second year than the first, but clearly persisted. Output per worker fell slightly, by about 3%, so unit cost rose by about 3.5%. In that trial, much of the gain ran through fewer recurring meetings. Whether this holds elsewhere, and whether the hours cut is needed to get it, are open questions. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added, at roughly 9% higher cost per unit in the one costed case. Sickness absence and resignations fell in every study that measured them; how much of the sickness fall reflects fewer working days is unmeasured.

Compared with my previous version, this one:
- reports the trial result as found;
- removes my unverified claims about the width of the confidence interval and an upper bound;
- moves the sick-day concern into a clearly marked open question.

**The most useful next step** is to have someone who hasn't read my reviews check this bottom line and the briefing against the five sources.
